steps.text: Part 2 of 3: Sure material, or a trap?. This part covers When the trap fails; Check before you capture. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

[I] Our working rule: a lure usually needs three things. It must look like a gain to someone counting material. The hidden reply must exist in *this* position: one missing piece can switch it off, as the knight on b1 showed. And the reply should come with tempo, like the check on the Nxd5 board, so the victim has no time to fix things.

steps.caption: Black to move: the first board of this lesson with one change. The white knight is back on b1 instead of c3. Watch what the missing knight changes.

line.say: Black takes the queen.
White checks with the bishop.
The king steps to e7.
The bishop takes the knight on g8, but no knight stands ready to jump to d5.
The rook takes the bishop.
The king takes the bishop on d1. Count: Black has the queen and a bishop for a pawn, a knight and a bishop, about five points up.

claims.statement: Bxd1 is the engine's first choice (depth 16).
The white knight is still on b1.
The white pawn is still on d2, so the position differs from the first board only by the knight.

steps.caption: White to move, the same position as before. Bxf7+ is the less bad capture: the engine still rates White about two thirds of a pawn worse (depth 16). The lure was a poor idea either way.

line.say: The bishop takes f7 with check, and the knight on e5 guards it.
The king steps to d8 and gives up the right to castle.
White castles and gets the rook into play.

claims.statement: The knight capture on f7 is at least 500 centipawns worse than the best move (depth 16).
Even the best move leaves White worse: White's point of view, at most -20 centipawns (depth 16).
Bxf7+ and O-O are the two best moves, within 60 centipawns of each other (depth 16).

steps.title: Same capture, three positions
steps.prompt: Original first: with Black's bishop on c5, taking on e7 was a trap. Now one thing changes in each position. Which one offers sure material, which one is still a trap, and which has nothing to take? Predict, then check.

steps.caption: White to move: the safe position of the test above. Black's bishop has not gone to c5, so the check in between does not exist.

line.say: The pawn takes the knight and attacks both the queen on d8 and the bishop on f8.
Black takes the pawn with the queen. White has won a knight for a pawn.

claims.statement: dxe7 is the engine's first choice (depth 16).
After dxe7 the white pawn on e7 attacks d8, where Black's queen stands.
After dxe7 the white pawn on e7 also attacks f8, where Black's bishop stands.

steps.text: **Other voices.** Dan Heisman calls moving without checking the opponent's forcing replies "Hope Chess" (chess.com article, [S]). Nimzowitsch warned against grabbing wing pawns before development is done, but allowed a centre pawn taken without great danger (*My System*, I.i §7, our wording). Capablanca shows traps beginners fall into, the first resembling the Légal pattern [I, our reading], yet advises taking sure material. [H] Guess: club traps work because the lure looks like an even trade.

steps.prompt: Do you agree with the guess [H]? Name one capture from your own games that looked like an even trade, and what you would check now.

fields.label: A capture from my games, and what I would check:

steps.text: **Before any capture, run two questions.** What does my capture open or take away? Which checks, captures and threats does the opponent have after it? [I] Rule of thumb: look at checks first, because they force your reply. If no forcing move hurts you, taking is usually right; the traps here were the exceptions. If one hurts, play a quiet move or work out why. Next: a safe capture with a check against it.

steps.caption: White to move. The pawn on e5 can be taken. Black's bishop has a check available on f2 after the capture, so run the two questions first.

line.say: The knight takes the pawn. Black has one check in reply, so look at it.
Black plays the check.
The king takes the bishop, which nothing defends.
Black checks again by taking the e-pawn with the knight.
The knight on c3 takes the checking knight.

claims.statement: Nxe5 is the engine's first choice (depth 16).
White stands at least 0.8 pawns better (White's point of view, depth 16).

steps.caption: White to move. Black has just recaptured on d4. Is there anything to check before taking back?

line.say: The queen takes the knight, and the piece is back.
Black attacks the queen and the pawn on f2.
White offers a queen trade.

claims.statement: Qxd4 is the engine's first choice (depth 16).
Declining with Nc3 is at least 400 centipawns worse (depth 16).

steps.caption: White to move. In our 1100-1300 sample 117 games reached this position and White chose the queen move in 100 of them (85%). Why is it so strong?

line.say: A quiet queen move aims along the long diagonal at the rook on a8 and along the f-file at f7.
Black blocks the diagonal with the knight, but the queen takes it with check.
The queen takes the knight with check.

claims.statement: Qf3 is the engine's first choice (depth 16).
After Qf3 the rook on a8 is loose.
After Qf3 Nc6 the white queen attacks the knight on c6.

steps.text: Every defence loses a piece or the rook (engine, depth 16, all about 4 pawns for White or more). [I] The reason: the rook on a8 is guarded only by the queen, and the knight and bishop on b8 and c8 block that guard. Quiet moves like this are the other side of a trap: nothing is offered, yet something is already lost.

steps.caption: Black to move, one move earlier. 117 of the 121 games that reached this position recaptured on b5. Here is a quiet developing move instead. Black is still a pawn down, about 1.9 pawns by the engine (depth 16); recapturing is worse still.

line.say: Black develops and leaves the pawn on c4 where it is.
White takes the pawn back with the bishop.
Black opens the bishop on c8 and keeps the queen's file clear.

claims.statement: Nf6, Bb7 and e6 are each within 40 centipawns of the engine's first choice (depth 16).
Recapturing on b5 is at least 200 centipawns worse (depth 16).

steps.caption: Black to move, and the knight on e4 is attacked by the white queen. In our 1100-1300 sample 51 of 574 games retreated the knight to f6, and White found the knight jump in 44 of those 51.

line.say: Black puts the knight back on its starting square, the move that feels natural.
The knight jumps with a discovered check from the queen on e2, and it also attacks the black queen.
Black blocks the check with the queen.
The knight takes the queen.
The bishop takes the knight. White has won a queen for a knight.

claims.statement: Retreating with Nf6 is at least 400 centipawns worse than the best move (depth 16).

steps.caption: Black to move, the same position. Here is the reply that avoids the discovered check. White keeps a small edge, about 0.6 pawns by the engine (depth 16).

line.say: Black puts the queen on the e-file and attacks the knight on e5 instead of retreating.
White takes the knight on e4. The knight on e5 now stands between the two queens, so it cannot move without exposing the queen.
Black attacks the knight on e5 with a pawn.
White supports the knight.
Black takes the knight.
White takes back. Knights are traded, and White is a pawn up.

claims.statement: Qe7 is the engine's first choice (depth 16).

steps.caption: White to move, and fxe5 is on the table. The remedy is not to avoid the capture for ever but to make the check harmless first.

line.say: A quiet pawn move that keeps the centre pawn protected and opens the bishop on c1.
Black prepares to develop the bishop.
The knight now covers h4, so a queen check there would simply lose the queen.
Black develops the bishop.
Now the capture is safe for the same reason.
Black recaptures with the pawn.

claims.statement: Nc3, d3 and Be2 are each within 40 centipawns of the engine's first choice (depth 16).
After d3 g6 Nf3 the white knight attacks h4.

steps.caption: White to move. Black's bishop pins the knight on f3 against the queen. A trap-setter's moves can look ordinary [I]: the knight to c3 is a developing move any book would give.

line.say: A normal developing move. It also puts a knight where it can later jump to d5.
Black plays a quiet move that leaves the pin alone.
The knight leaves the pin on purpose: the queen is attacked, and the lure is set.

claims.statement: After Nxe5 the black bishop attacks the white queen on d1.
